claim: Female Platynereis dumerilii committed to reproduction spend roughly half their body mass for yolk and egg production.
source: females committed to reproduction spend roughly half their body mass for yolk and egg production
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a factual assertion about the reproductive biology of the species.

claim: Following mass spawning, Platynereis dumerilii parents die.
source: following mass spawning, the parents die
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characteristic of the species' reproductive strategy.

claim: An enigmatic brain hormone activity suppresses reproduction in Platynereis dumerilii.
source: An enigmatic brain hormone activity suppresses reproduction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by classical experiments described in the introduction.

claim: Methylfarnesoate is the brain hormone that suppresses reproduction in Platynereis dumerilii.
source: We now identify this hormone as the sesquiterpenoid methylfarnesoate.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by biochemical purification, mass spectrometry, and functional assays.

claim: Methylfarnesoate suppresses transcript levels of Vitellogenin in cell culture.
source: Methylfarnesoate suppresses transcript levels of the yolk precursor Vitellogenin both in cell culture and in vivo
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR experiments in primary coelomocyte cultures shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Methylfarnesoate suppresses transcript levels of Vitellogenin in vivo.
source: Methylfarnesoate suppresses transcript levels of the yolk precursor Vitellogenin both in cell culture and in vivo
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR experiments in decapitated animals treated with MF shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Sesquiterpenoids are ancient animal hormones present in marine and terrestrial lophotrochozoans.
source: We reveal that contrary to common assumptions, sesquiterpenoids are ancient animal hormones present in marine and terrestrial lophotrochozoans.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of MF in Platynereis and earthworms, and the identification of Met orthologues in molluscs.

claim: Insecticides targeting the sesquiterpenoid pathway suppress vitellogenesis in cultured Platynereis cells.
source: In turn, insecticides targeting this pathway suppress vitellogenesis in cultured worm cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that methoprene and pyriproxyfen reduce vtg levels in coelomocyte cultures (Figure 5).

claim: Non-target species and marine ecosystems are susceptible to commonly used insect larvicides.
source: These findings challenge current views of animal hormone evolution, and indicate that non-target species and marine ecosystems are susceptible to commonly used insect larvicides.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that insecticides targeting sesquiterpenoid signaling affect Platynereis vitellogenesis.

claim: Migrating salmon break down about 50% of their white muscle mass during maturation.
source: migrating salmon break down about 50% of their white muscle mass while their gonad mass multiplies around six-fold during maturation (Mommsen, 2004)
evidence: This is cited from Mommsen, 2004 as an example of extreme energy expenditure in semelparous animals.

claim: Salmon gonad mass multiplies around six-fold during maturation.
source: migrating salmon break down about 50% of their white muscle mass while their gonad mass multiplies around six-fold during maturation (Mommsen, 2004)
evidence: This is cited from Mommsen, 2004 as an example of extreme energy expenditure in semelparous animals.

claim: Female squids exhibit almost complete histolysis of mantle muscle during maturation.
source: Likewise, female squids exhibit almost complete histolysis of mantle muscle (Jackson and Mladenov, 1994)
evidence: This is cited from Jackson and Mladenov, 1994 as an example of extreme energy expenditure in semelparous animals.

claim: In mature female squids, up to ~60% of the total body mass at spawning consists of eggs.
source: in mature female squids up to ~60% of the total body mass at spawning consists of eggs (Rodrigues et al., 2011)
evidence: This is cited from Rodrigues et al., 2011 as an example of extreme energy expenditure in semelparous animals.

claim: In Nereis virens, oocytes represent up to about 40% of the body mass of the spawning adult.
source: Similarly, in the marine annelid worm Nereis virens, oocytes represent up to about 40% of the body mass of the spawning adult (Hoeger et al., 1999)
evidence: This is cited from Hoeger et al., 1999 as an example of extreme energy expenditure in semelparous annelids.

claim: Platynereis dumerilii is a semelparous animal that can easily be reared in the laboratory.
source: In this study, we explore the marine annelid Platynereis dumerilii, a semelparous animal that can easily be reared in the laboratory (Hauenschild and Fischer, 1969; Fischer and Dorresteijn, 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to laboratory culture methods.

claim: Platynereis dumerilii has been established as a molecular model system over the last decade.
source: has been established as a molecular model system over the last decade (reviewed in Zantke et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a review citation.

claim: Platynereis has retained various ancient-type characteristics.
source: A series of studies show that Platynereis has retained various ancient-type characteristics (Arendt et al., 2004; Raible et al., 2005; Denes et al., 2007; Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007; Keay and Thornton, 2009; Christodoulou et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Decerebration of Platynereis leads to accelerated sexual maturation.
source: Decerebration of Platynereis leads to an accelerated sexual maturation and to the loss of regenerative abilities, whereas re-implantation of a juvenile head with neuroendocrine activity is able to reverse these effects (Hauenschild, 1956a, 1956b, 1960, 1966)
evidence: This is cited from classical experiments by Hauenschild.

claim: Decerebration of Platynereis leads to loss of regenerative abilities.
source: Decerebration of Platynereis leads to an accelerated sexual maturation and to the loss of regenerative abilities, whereas re-implantation of a juvenile head with neuroendocrine activity is able to reverse these effects (Hauenschild, 1956a, 1956b, 1960, 1966)
evidence: This is cited from classical experiments by Hauenschild.

claim: Re-implantation of a juvenile head with neuroendocrine activity can reverse the effects of decerebration in Platynereis.
source: Decerebration of Platynereis leads to an accelerated sexual maturation and to the loss of regenerative abilities, whereas re-implantation of a juvenile head with neuroendocrine activity is able to reverse these effects (Hauenschild, 1956a, 1956b, 1960, 1966)
evidence: This is cited from classical experiments by Hauenschild.

claim: In Nereis diversicolor, implantation of ganglia from immature animals into maturing animals reversed the effects of decreasing nereidin concentration.
source: In the related species Nereis diversicolor, it could be shown that implantation of ganglia from immature animals into the coelomic cavity of maturing animals, reversed the effects of the decreasing nereidin concentration. In particular, germ cells were resorbed and the ability to regenerate lost segments was re-established (Golding and Yuwono, 1994)
evidence: This is cited from Golding and Yuwono, 1994.

claim: In Nereis diversicolor, implantation of ganglia from immature animals caused germ cells to be resorbed.
source: In the related species Nereis diversicolor, it could be shown that implantation of ganglia from immature animals into the coelomic cavity of maturing animals, reversed the effects of the decreasing nereidin concentration. In particular, germ cells were resorbed and the ability to regenerate lost segments was re-established (Golding and Yuwono, 1994)
evidence: This is cited from Golding and Yuwono, 1994.

claim: In Nereis diversicolor, implantation of ganglia from immature animals re-established the ability to regenerate lost segments.
source: In the related species Nereis diversicolor, it could be shown that implantation of ganglia from immature animals into the coelomic cavity of maturing animals, reversed the effects of the decreasing nereidin concentration. In particular, germ cells were resorbed and the ability to regenerate lost segments was re-established (Golding and Yuwono, 1994)
evidence: This is cited from Golding and Yuwono, 1994.

claim: Nereidin-like activities have been identified in various annelids.
source: As Nereidin-like activities have been identified in various annelids, this suggests that these substances could be chemically related.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on classical literature.

claim: Histological analyses of the proposed biosynthetically active brain region were compatible with the hypothesis that nereidin is a neuropeptide.
source: Histological analyses of the proposed biosynthetically active brain region (Müller, 1973; Hofmann, 1976) were compatible with a fourth hypothesis, namely that nereidin is a neuropeptide.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to histological studies.

claim: Large-scale purifications of nereidin have been performed from head extracts of Nereis diversicolor and Perinereis cultrifera.
source: Based on this hypothesis, large-scale purifications have been performed from head extracts of N. diversicolor and Perinereis cultrifera (Cardon et al., 1981)
evidence: This is cited from Cardon et al., 1981.

claim: A hexapeptide (PPGPPG) was identified from nereidin purifications but did not display biological activity.
source: These finally resulted in the identification of a hexapeptide (PPGPPG). However, this peptide did not display biological activity (Durchon, 1984)
evidence: This is cited from Durchon, 1984.

claim: Vitellogenin transcript levels in Platynereis eleocytes increase over female maturation.
source: Indeed, we found a strong correlation between vtg-transcript abundance in eleocytes and the maturation state of the animal (as assessed by oocyte diameter, Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Vitellogenin is synthesised in coelomic cells called eleocytes.
source: Vtg is synthesised in coelomic cells called eleocytes (Figure 1B) that are present in large numbers (Baert and Slomianny, 1987; Hoeger, 1991)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: Vitellogenin is derived by endocytotic uptake into the oocyte.
source: Yolk protein is derived by endocytotic uptake of Vtg into the oocyte (Fischer et al., 1991)
evidence: This is cited from Fischer et al., 1991.

claim: Vitellogenin accounts for more than 40% of protein in Platynereis oocytes.
source: Yolk protein is derived by endocytotic uptake of Vtg into the oocyte (Fischer et al., 1991), where it accounts for more than 40% of protein (Fischer and Schmitz, 1981)
evidence: This is cited from Fischer and Schmitz, 1981.

claim: The 50% methanol eluate of phenyl-SPE column fractionation of Platynereis head extracts showed clear nereidin activity.
source: Consistent with previous characterisations of nereidin, the 50% methanol eluate of this column showed clear activity (Figure 2B) when added to coelomocytes in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the bioassay results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Nereidin activity is not sensitive to proteinase treatment.
source: Our results demonstrate that nereidin is insensitive to proteinase K-treatment, thus strongly arguing against the notion that it is a neuropeptide hormone (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the proteinase K treatment experiment shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Peak 15 from C18-reverse phase column chromatography of head extracts significantly suppresses vtg levels in the coelomocyte bioassay.
source: One peak (peak 15) could be identified that robustly and significantly reduced vtg transcripts in two independent experiments and showed a reasonable chromatographic purity (Figure 2D,E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the bioassay results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Analysis of peak 15 by LC-MS/MS clearly demonstrated the presence of methylfarnesoate.
source: Analysis of peak 15 by LC-MS/MS clearly demonstrated the presence of the sesquiterpenoid methylfarnesoate (MF), when compared to an authentic standard run under the same conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Authentic methylfarnesoate down-regulates vtg transcript levels in cell culture assays.
source: The results showed a clear down-regulation of vtg transcript levels (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the bioassay results shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Methylfarnesoate shows strongest effects on vtg levels in the range between 1 and 100 nM.
source: Strongest effects were observed in the range between 1 and 100 nM MF, in agreement with physiological concentrations expected for a hormone.
evidence: This is observed from the dose-response data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Palmitic acid does not show a significant effect on vitellogenesis in coelomocyte cultures.
source: As evident from Figure 2G, neither of these molecules showed a significant effect on vitellogenesis, thus establishing the specificity of MF on the observed reduction of vtg transcript levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the specificity experiment shown in Figure 2G.

claim: All-trans-retinoic acid does not show a significant effect on vitellogenesis in coelomocyte cultures.
source: As evident from Figure 2G, neither of these molecules showed a significant effect on vitellogenesis, thus establishing the specificity of MF on the observed reduction of vtg transcript levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the specificity experiment shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Heads of premature Platynereis animals contain ~5510 ± 660 pg MF/mg protein.
source: Heads of premature animals were determined to possess ~5510 ± 660 pg MF/mg protein (mean±standard error of the mean)
evidence: This is measured by GC-MS quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Heads of mature Platynereis animals contain ~2870 ± 495 pg MF/mg protein.
source: whereas concentrations in the heads of mature animals were found to be significantly lower (~2870 ± 495 pg MF/mg protein)
evidence: This is measured by GC-MS quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Methylfarnesoate levels in Platynereis heads decrease significantly between premature and mature stages.
source: Measuring MF levels present in heads of different developmental stages showed differences in MF content (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by GC-MS quantification shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Premature Platynereis heads contain ~34.6 ± 8.0 pg MF per head.
source: Calculated per head, the MF content is equivalent to ~34.6 ± 8.0 pg/head for premature heads
evidence: This is calculated from GC-MS quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mature Platynereis heads contain ~15.4 ± 2.5 pg MF per head.
source: and ~15.4 ± 2.5 pg/head for mature animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is calculated from GC-MS quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Platynereis possesses an orthologue of arthropod sesquiterpenoid receptors Methoprene-tolerant (Met) and Germ cells expressed (Gce).
source: Molecular phylogeny revealed this protein to be a clear orthologue of the insect Methoprene-tolerant and germ cell expressed (Gce) receptors, as well as the functionally confirmed Met receptors from the crustacean Daphnia.
evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Met orthologues exist in the molluscs Lottia gigantea and Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: The phylogenetic analysis also revealed Met orthologues in the molluscs Lottia gigantea and Lymnaea stagnalis (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Platynereis met is expressed in eleocytes.
source: Using qRT-PCR analysis, we could confirm the expression of Platynereis met in eleocytes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression level of Platynereis met in eleocytes drops significantly during maturation to ~61% of the level in premature animals.
source: Furthermore, these analyses revealed that the expression level of this gene dropped significantly during maturation, reaching only ~ 61% of the level observed in cells from premature animals (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Treatment of cultured premature eleocytes with 10 nM MF induced a 30% up-regulation of Platynereis met expression.
source: Furthermore, treatment of cultured premature eleocytes with 10 nM MF induced the expression of Platynereis met, resulting in a 30% up-regulation (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Decapitation of Platynereis leads to accelerated maturation.
source: Decapitation leads to accelerated maturation, and, importantly, synchronisation of maturation across different individuals (Hauenschild, 1966, 1974)
evidence: This is cited from classical experiments by Hauenschild.

claim: Decapitation of Platynereis leads to synchronisation of maturation across different individuals.
source: Decapitation leads to accelerated maturation, and, importantly, synchronisation of maturation across different individuals (Hauenschild, 1966, 1974)
evidence: This is cited from classical experiments by Hauenschild.

claim: Vitellogenin levels in decapitated Platynereis animals treated with MF are ~70% lower than in control animals.
source: Expression levels of vtg upon presence of MF are ~70% lower than in treated animals.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis of decapitated animals shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Methylfarnesoate exerts a repressive effect on vitellogenesis in vivo.
source: The results of these experiments showed that vtg levels were strongly down-regulated in MF-treated worms when compared to a non-treated control group (Figure 4B). This establishes that MF does not only have an effect on isolated coelomocytes, but also exerts a similar effect in vivo
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Methoprene at 10 nM significantly decreases vtg levels in Platynereis eleocyte cultures.
source: In this experimental setup, we did not observe a significant decrease in vtg levels. In contrast, applying methoprene to eleocytes in our cell culture assay clearly led to reduced vtg levels at a concentration of 10 nM (Figure 5)
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell culture experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Pyriproxyfen at 10 nM significantly decreases vtg levels in Platynereis eleocyte cultures.
source: Indeed, when applying pyriproxyfen at the same concentration (10 nM), we again observed a significant decrease in the abundance of vtg transcripts when compared to controls.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell culture experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Expression of hox3 is significantly up-regulated (~2 fold) in Platynereis fragments treated with 100 nM MF compared to control fragments after 5 days.
source: Our results show that the expression of hox3 is significantly up-regulated (~2 fold) after 5 days in test fragments treated with 100 nM MF when compared to DMSO-treated control fragments (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hox3 expression is a highly specific early marker in caudal regeneration of Platynereis.
source: Hox3 expression has earlier been demonstrated to be a highly specific early on marker in caudal regeneration (Pfeifer et al., 2012)
evidence: This is cited from Pfeifer et al., 2012.

claim: Hox3 has been linked to ectodermal cells of likely stem cell character (ectoteleoblasts) involved in the regenerative process.
source: More specifically, it has recently been linked to ectodermal cells of likely stem cell character (ectoteleoblasts, Gazave et al., 2013) involved in the regenerative process.
evidence: This is cited from Gazave et al., 2013.

claim: The ability of MF to suppress vtg levels is compatible with a central role of this compound in controlling reproduction-associated energy expenditure.
source: in light of the massive amounts of Vitellogenin that are produced by animals committed to reproduction, the ability of MF to suppress vtg levels is compatible with a central role of this compound in controlling reproduction-associated energy expenditure, as expected for nereidin
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and the known role of vitellogenin.

claim: The quantifications of MF levels over the course of reproductive development are consistent with the decline in nereidin activity present in transplanted heads of different stages.
source: Likewise, our quantifications of MF levels over the course of reproductive development (Figure 3A) are consistent with the decline in nereidin activity present in transplanted heads of different stages.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the measured MF levels to classical nereidin activity assays.

claim: The data are consistent with the chemical properties (apparent mass, lipophilic nature) that have been derived from previous purification attempts of nereidin.
source: Although our data clearly argue against the long-held assumption that nereidin is a neuropeptide, they are still consistent with the chemical properties (apparent mass, lipophilic nature) that have been derived from previous purification attempts.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the properties of MF to previous characterizations of nereidin.

claim: Eleocytes are direct target cells for methylfarnesoate.
source: We show that eleocytes are direct target cells for MF, indicating a direct cross-talk between the brain and a highly relevant metabolic cell type.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression of Met in eleocytes and the direct effect of MF on vtg levels in eleocyte cultures.

claim: The observed effect of MF on vitellogenin levels is consistent with a direct function of MF in controlling this key factor for oocyte maturation.
source: Moreover, the observed effect of MF on vitellogenin levels is consistent with a direct function of MF in controlling this key factor for oocyte maturation.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results showing MF suppresses vtg levels.

claim: The positive autoregulation of the sesquiterpenoid receptor orthologue Met is reminiscent of other hormone ligand-receptor systems, such as thyroxin or ecdysone.
source: The positive autoregulation of the sesquiterpenoid receptor orthologue Met that we observe is reminiscent of other hormone ligand-receptor systems, such as thyroxin or ecdysone (Thummel, 1995; Bagamasbad and Denver, 2011)
evidence: This is a comparison to other known hormone systems, supported by citations.

claim: The discovery of MF in Platynereis heads challenges the hypothesis that nereidin is a peptide.
source: The identification of MF in Platynereis heads challenges several hypotheses: most directly, it defeats the hypothesis that nereidin is a peptide, a notion that has been propagated in the literature for more than 30 years (Cardon et al., 1981; Durchon, 1984)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a direct consequence of the findings.

claim: MF and related sesquiterpenoid hormones have so far only been found in arthropods.
source: Furthermore, MF and related sesquiterpenoid hormones have so far only been found in arthropods (Bellés et al., 2005; Jindra et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated as the prevailing view before this study, supported by citations.

claim: The evolution of sesquiterpenoid hormones has been hypothesised to be a secondary consequence of the loss of the sterol synthesis pathway in arthropods.
source: and their evolution has been hypothesised to be a secondary consequence of the loss of the sterol synthesis pathway in this clade (Zandee, 1964; Bellés et al., 2005)
evidence: This is stated as a previous hypothesis, supported by citations.

claim: Marine nereidid worms possess a functional sterol synthesis pathway.
source: As marine nereidid worms were previously shown to possess a functional sterol synthesis pathway (Wootton and Wright, 1962)
evidence: This is cited from Wootton and Wright, 1962.

claim: Platynereis has a functional estrogen receptor.
source: and Platynereis even has a functional estrogen receptor (Keay and Thornton, 2009)
evidence: This is cited from Keay and Thornton, 2009.

claim: Loss of sterol synthesis did not precede the evolution of sesquiterpenoid hormones.
source: our discovery makes it unlikely that loss of sterol synthesis preceded the evolution of sesquiterpenoid hormones
evidence: This is an inference from the finding of MF in Platynereis, which has sterol synthesis.

claim: Bioactive sesquiterpenoids could have been part of the ancient molecular repertoire available in the common ancestor of protostomes.
source: Rather, it suggests that, like sterols, bioactive sesquiterpenoids, could have been part of the ancient molecular repertoire available in the common ancestor of protostomes, if not even at earlier stages of animal evolution.
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetic distribution of sesquiterpenoid signaling components.

claim: Exogenous MF affects larval development of the annelid Capitella sp.
source: Exogenous MF was found to affect larval development of the annelid Capitella sp. (Laufer and Biggers, 2001)
evidence: This is cited from Laufer and Biggers, 2001.

claim: Annelid extracts displayed biological activity in assays for insect juvenile hormones.
source: and annelid extracts displayed biological activity in assays for insect juvenile hormones (Schneiderman and Gilbert, 1958)
evidence: This is cited from Schneiderman and Gilbert, 1958.

claim: Methylfarnesoate has been detected in head extracts of common earthworms (Lumbricus sp.).
source: Moreover, we have detected MF in head extracts of common earthworms (Lumbricus sp., Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is demonstrated by GC-MS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The sesquiterpenoid signalling pathway might exist in molluscs.
source: Beyond the annelid clade, our identification of Methoprene-tolerant orthologues in the limpet Lottia and the pond snail Lymnaea indicates that the sesquiterpenoid signalling pathway might even exist in molluscs.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic identification of Met orthologues in molluscs.

claim: Annelids and molluscs are large groups within the lophotrochozoan superphylum.
source: As annelids and molluscs are large groups within the lophotrochozoan superphylum (Halanych et al., 1995)
evidence: This is cited from Halanych et al., 1995.

claim: Sesquiterpenoids have a potential physiological role in a broad set of (mostly aquatic) species.
source: this implies a potential physiological role for sesquiterpenoids in a broad set of (mostly aquatic) species
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of sesquiterpenoid signaling in lophotrochozoans.

claim: Semelparity is considered an extreme form of 'capital breeding'.
source: Semelparity, as it occurs in Platynereis, is considered an extreme form of 'capital breeding', a reproductive strategy where females build up large energy stores in their bodies that are then invested into offspring at particular time points (Drent and Daan, 1980)
evidence: This is cited from Drent and Daan, 1980.

claim: Capital breeding likely represents an ancient reproductive strategy that is very common in poikilothermic animals.
source: It likely represents an ancient reproductive strategy that is very common in poikilothermic animals (Bonnet et al., 1998)
evidence: This is cited from Bonnet et al., 1998.

claim: The inhibitory function of MF for maturation in Platynereis is reminiscent of the juvenoid functions of insect juvenile hormones.
source: The inhibitory function for maturation we uncover in Platynereis is reminiscent of the juvenoid functions of insect juvenile hormones: During pre-adult development, these provide a molecular cue for juvenile status, preventing insects from entering into adulthood, and thereby indirectly preventing reproductive energy expenditure as well.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn between the function of MF in Platynereis and juvenile hormones in insects.

claim: MF treatment of larval stages of crustaceans can delay metamorphosis or prevent gonad formation.
source: Likewise, MF treatment of larval stages of crustaceans can delay metamorphosis or prevent gonad formation (Borst et al., 1987; Tsukimura et al., 2006)
evidence: This is cited from Borst et al., 1987 and Tsukimura et al., 2006.

claim: Juvenile hormones commonly act as positive regulators of vitellogenesis in the adult insect fat body.
source: In contrast to our results in worms, juvenile hormones commonly act as positive regulators of vitellogenesis in the adult insect fat body, whereas their down-regulation is associated with diapause and longevity (Gäde et al., 1997; Wyatt, 1997; Hansen et al., 2014)
evidence: This is cited from Gäde et al., 1997; Wyatt, 1997; Hansen et al., 2014.

claim: MF promotes adult maturation, vitellogenesis and mating behaviour in crustaceans.
source: Similarly, MF promotes adult maturation, vitellogenesis and mating behaviour in crustaceans (Laufer et al., 1987; Homola and Chang, 1997; Subramoniam, 2011)
evidence: This is cited from Laufer et al., 1987; Homola and Chang, 1997; Subramoniam, 2011.

claim: MF has a separate function in sex determination in crustaceans.
source: with a separate function in sex determination (Toyota et al., 2015)
evidence: This is cited from Toyota et al., 2015.

claim: Platynereis retains certain MF levels even in the mature stage.
source: As Platynereis retains certain MF levels even in the mature stage (see above)
evidence: This is observed from the GC-MS quantification data showing MF is still present in mature heads.

claim: Juvenile hormone analogues like methoprene and pyriproxyfen are broadly used to fight insect pests such as Aedes.
source: Juvenile hormone analogues like methoprene and later pyriproxyfen have initially been designed to interfere with insect development and are broadly used to fight insect pests such as Aedes, a vector for dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever viruses (reviewed in Henrick, 2007)
evidence: This is cited from a review by Henrick, 2007.

claim: The discovery of sesquiterpenoid MF in crustaceans raised concerns if the effect of juvenile hormone analogues is restricted to insect development.
source: The discovery the sesquiterpenoid MF in crustaceans by Laufer et al. (1987) already raised concerns if the effect of juvenile hormone analogues is restricted to insect development (Walker et al., 2005; Abe et al., 2015)
evidence: This is cited from Laufer et al., 1987; Walker et al., 2005; Abe et al., 2015.

claim: Aquatic lophotrochozoans should be systematically included in specificity tests for compounds targeting sesquiterpenoid signalling pathway.
source: Our results argue that aquatic lophotrochozoans should also be systematically included in specificity tests for compounds targeting sesquiterpenoid signalling pathway
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings that sesquiterpenoid signaling exists in lophotrochozoans.

claim: Tests for compounds targeting sesquiterpenoid signalling should not be restricted to mortality, but include assays on reproductive fitness.
source: and that such tests should not be restricted to mortality (Henrick, 2007), but include assays on reproductive fitness
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the finding that MF affects vitellogenesis, a reproductive process.

claim: Pyriproxyfen impacts on vtg levels at concentrations of 10 nM which lies in the range of pyriproxyfen found in surface waters.
source: For instance, in our studies, pyriproxyfen impacts on vtg levels at concentrations of 10 nM which lies in the range of pyriproxyfen found in surface waters (Sullivan and Goh, 2008)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to Sullivan and Goh, 2008.

claim: The Platynereis protein encoded by the identified cDNA shares three conserved domains with other bilaterian Vitellogenins arranged in the same order.
source: Domain analysis for the protein encoded by the identified Platynereis cDNA (top) as well as chicken Vtg2 (middle) and mosquito Vit1 (bottom) reveals that Platynereis Vtg shares three conserved domains with other bilaterian Vitellogenins that are arranged in the same order: a Lipoprotein N-terminal Domain (LPD-N, SMART accession SM000638, blue), a DUF1943 domain (DUF, SMART accession SM001169, green), and a van Willebrand factor D domain (VW, SMART accession SM000216, red).
evidence: This is demonstrated by domain analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Molecular phylogenetic analysis supports the orthology of Platynereis Vtg with representatives of other invertebrate and vertebrate Vitellogenins.
source: Molecular phylogenetic analysis supports the orthology of Platynereis Vtg with representatives of other invertebrate and vertebrate Vitellogenins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The extraction efficiency of the MF quantification method was determined to be >85%.
source: The extraction efficiency of our method was determined to be >85%.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section based on spike-in experiments.
